name: Soba

cells.flour: Three houses: Sarashina (white first-milling), Yabu, Sunaba; 'ni-hachi' 8:2 with wheat
cells.serving: Cold on a bamboo tray (mori / zaru), or hot in broth (kake)
cells.sauce: Strong dark 'kaeshi' soy with bonito; dip only halfway
cells.howToEat: Slurp; finish with soba-yu, the cooking water, in the leftover sauce

origin.era: station soba known by c. 1897 (one theory); chains from 1966

cells.serving: At a counter, standing: hot kake or cold mori, tempura soba on the same menu
cells.sauce: Kanto stock is mostly bonito-based; two counters of one Shinagawa caterer make it to different strengths
cells.howToEat: Often between trains; Fuji Soba kake ¥450 tax included (Oct 2026)

cells.flour: Hikigurumi — whole grain milled with the husk: dark, fragrant; about 20% wheat
cells.serving: Wariko: three stacked round red-lacquer dishes; or kama-age in its cooking water
cells.sauce: Poured over the noodles, not dipped; passed down from dish to dish
cells.howToEat: Grated daikon with chilli; the cooking water is part of the dish

origin.era: Heian-era mountain ascetics; soba-kiri in the Edo period

cells.serving: 'Botchi-mori': five or six horseshoe-shaped bundles on a round bamboo tray, barely drained
cells.howToEat: A shrine offering turned hospitality dish

cells.serving: A server refills a small lacquer bowl until you close the lid
cells.sauce: Pre-sauced; condiments change the bowl as you go
cells.howToEat: 15 bowls ≈ one normal serving; the record is 632

cells.flour: Historically flour paid to the temple by farmers in place of rice; stone-milled
cells.serving: Mori (seiro at some shops, zaru with nori) and hot bowls; tempura soba usually with prawn
cells.sauce: Dipping sauce, thinned with soba-yu after the meal
cells.howToEat: Spring onion and wasabi, shichimi to taste; many shops close with the temple gate at about 5 p.m.

cells.flour: Bound with funori seaweed, once used to stiffen loom threads
cells.serving: On a hegi, a square tray of split wood
cells.howToEat: Spring onion and mustard, not wasabi; mostly at soba shops

origin.era: Asakura era from 1473 (held to be); Honda Tomimasa from 1601

cells.flour: Thin soba, in the ministry's account
cells.serving: Cold, with grated daikon; at weddings, memorials, New Year's Eve and hōonkō
cells.sauce: Three ways: broth and daikon apart, daikon in the broth, or daikon juice in the broth
cells.howToEat: Paired with sauce katsudon eating out; soba-making session ¥2,200 tax included (Oct 2026)

cells.serving: At home or by delivery, on 31 December
cells.howToEat: Eaten by more than 60% of households; long for long life, easily cut to cut off the year's troubles
